title: You speak more Latin than you think.

entries.note: From [[from:Latinus]], meaning of [[from:Latium]], the region where Rome stood; it appears in Old English as the name for the language of the Romans.
The ancient region covering Rome and the lower Tiber, home of the Latins, which gave its name to [[gave:Latin]]; modern Italians call it [[see:Lazio]].
The modern Italian name for [[see:Latium]], familiar to football fans from the team called Lazio.
Borrowed from Old French, from late Latin for in the Roman manner; it names the Romance languages descended from Latin and, more loosely, novels celebrating the classics.
Taken from the Romans by the Germanic dialects before English existed, so English has always had the word.
Like [[see:wine]], picked up from the Romans by the Germanic dialects before English formed in Britain.
Long in English, from Latin [[from:mille passus]], a thousand paces, because a Roman mile was a thousand paces long.
Originally in the sense of a battle, from Latin on the continent before English existed; related to German [[same-root:Kampf]], [[same-root:campaign]] and [[same-root:champion]].
German word related to [[same-root:camp]], famous from the title of Hitler's book.
Related to [[same-root:camp]] but adopted later from French, one of many doublets from borrowing the same word repeatedly.
Related to [[same-root:camp]] but adopted later from French.
Borrowed before English existed, from Latin strata, as in [[from:via strata]], a straight road, so street essentially means straight.
From Latin [[from:vallum]], pronounced with a W sound in [[see:classical Latin]].
Pronounced V as W and C as K, unlike [[see:ecclesiastical Latin]]; Rob jokes he was speaking the latter when he said via strata.
Pronounces V and C more as they look to English speakers, unlike [[see:classical Latin]].
From Latin [[from:castellum]], a fort or stronghold, entering late Old English often through biblical usage; later borrowed again as [[same-root:chateau]].
A second borrowing of the word behind [[same-root:castle]], probably later than the Normans because it looks almost too perfectly French.
From Latin [[from:altare]], thought to come not from [[unrelated?:altus]], high, but from [[from?:adolere]], to burn, since sacrifices were burned there.
One of the Latin words Christian missionaries brought to the Anglo-Saxons.
From Latin [[from:scrinium]], a chest, then a chest holding a relic such as a saint's body parts, then a venerated place itself.
Another Latin word that Christian missionaries brought to the Anglo-Saxons.
Ultimately from Latin [[from:pulvinus]], little cushion, perhaps reaching other Germanic languages first; Rob finds it hard to imagine people using pillows back then.
Latin for way, road, path or course, hidden in English words like [[gave:obvious]], [[gave:impervious]], [[gave:trivia]] and [[gave:invoice]].
One of the words with a root meaning to talk that Jess gave a fifth-grade class, who already knew it.
Guessed by Jess's fifth graders from [[same-root:eloquent]] and [[same-root:soliloquy]], which share its root meaning to talk.
Literally big talking, as the fifth graders worked out; [[see:William Barnes]] rendered it as [[see:high talking]].
Known to some of Jess's fifth graders; it shares a root meaning to speak with [[same-root:eloquent]].
Sleep talking, which the fifth graders worked out once Jess asked them what [[same-root:insomnia]] meant.
The clue that helped Jess's class decode [[same-root:somniloquy]].
Literally in the way or in front of you on the road, from [[from:via]]; so clear you might trip over it.
Im-, not, per, through, and [[from:via]], road: resistant to attack because there's no way through it.
Built on [[from:via]]: occurring earlier on your route or path.
To stray away from the course, from [[from:via]].
Straying from the moral path, built on [[from:via]] like [[same-root:deviant]].
Straying from the moral path, built on [[from:via]] like [[same-root:devious]].
Shaped by French but from [[from:viaticum]], a journey, part of the family of [[same-root:via]].
To carry something with you along a road, from [[from:via]].
Someone sent somewhere to represent someone else, from [[from:via]] and related to [[same-root:invoice]].
A request to send along a payment, related to [[same-root:envoy]]; it holds a road, [[from:via]], and is unrelated to [[unrelated:voice]].
From [[from:via]]: three roads, a junction where Romans traded goods and news; the fun-fact sense dates from [[see:Logan Pearsall Smith]]'s 1902 book series Trivia.
Describes inconsequential street talk, like the commoners' chatter at the Roman crossroads of [[from:trivia]].
The three classical arts of grammar, logic and rhetoric, studied before the [[see:quadrivium]]; coined in the Carolingian Renaissance and the basis of today's liberal arts.
The more advanced studies after the [[see:trivium]]: arithmetic, astronomy, music and geometry; the older of the two terms.
Writer known for clever sayings and essays whose 1902 book series Trivia, full of observations on public life, gave [[see:trivia]] its fun-fact sense.
Latin for to hang; Jess strings fourteen of its English descendants into one passage, from [[gave:pendulum]] to [[gave:pensive]] and [[gave:ponder]].
One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]], to hang, in Jess's passage.

One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]] in Jess's passage; Rob is struck that it shares an origin with [[same-root:pensive]].

From [[from:pensare]], to weigh or consider, a frequentative of [[from:pendere]]; something hanging on your mind, so it shares an origin with [[same-root:pendulum]].
Rob's favourite of the [[from:pendere]] words, spelled the way a French speaker might say it; from Latin [[from:ponderare]], to weigh.
From [[from:libra pondo]], pondo meaning weight, so pounds are weighty, hanging things related to [[same-root:ponder]].
Another hugely productive Latin root, meaning to hold, found in [[gave:maintain]], [[gave:abstain]], [[gave:entertain]], [[gave:obtain]] and [[gave:detain]].
One of the English words built on [[from:tenere]], to hold.
One of the English words built on [[from:tenere]], to hold.
One of the English words built on [[from:tenere]], to hold.
One of the English words built on [[from:tenere]], to hold.
From [[from:tenere]]: literally to hold in the hand, showing how literal these Latin compounds are.
The plain Old English word, contrasted with the weightier Latinate [[see:cardiovascular system]] used to be taken seriously in medicine.
The Latin-based term preferred over heart and vein system because it sounds more serious, an example of English's fancy Latin layer above Old English [[see:heart]].
A blunt German body-part word the hosts have discussed before, raised when Rob wishes German used more Latin terms.
Name for the backlash against Renaissance classical borrowings, perhaps because long words needed repeated dips in an inkhorn of ink; [[see:Sir John Cheke]] was a proponent.
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to, now taken for granted.
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to, now taken for granted.
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to.
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to, now taken for granted.
[[see:inkhorn]] purist who wrote the Gospel of Matthew without excessive borrowings, using [[see:hundreder]], [[see:crossed]] and [[see:outpeopling]], though plenty of borrowed words remained.
[[see:Sir John Cheke]]'s native replacement for [[see:centurion]] when writing about Romans.
The borrowed word [[see:Sir John Cheke]] replaced with [[see:hundreder]].
[[see:Sir John Cheke]]'s word for [[see:crucified]], which Jess says sounds like a euphemism and Rob notes clashes with crossing someone.
The word [[see:Sir John Cheke]] replaced with [[see:crossed]].
[[see:Sir John Cheke]]'s coinage in his Gospel of Matthew; the hosts guess it stands for [[see:diaspora]] or [[see:Exodus]] and note it's no shorter.
Coiner of Germanic alternatives like [[see:star lore]], [[see:bird lore]] and [[see:high talking]], whom Jess has mentioned before and prefers to [[see:Sir John Cheke]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s Germanic replacement for [[see:astronomy]].
The classical word [[see:William Barnes]] replaced with [[see:star lore]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s Germanic replacement for [[see:ornithology]].
The classical word [[see:William Barnes]] replaced with [[see:bird lore]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s Germanic rendering of [[see:grandiloquent]], which Jess likes.
An [[see:inkhorn]]-era native alternative, first said to replace [[see:knowledge]] but actually used for [[see:logic]], closer to the original meaning of wit.
Wrongly given as the word [[see:witcraft]] replaced, until Jess pointed out that know is already Germanic.
The word [[see:witcraft]] actually replaced; it comes from [[from:logos]], reason or idea.
A French word, so purists replacing [[see:logic]] couldn't use it and went back to [[see:witcraft]].
A French word, so purists replacing [[see:logic]] couldn't use it and went back to [[see:witcraft]].
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists as basic and easy to guess.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists, alongside its variant com-.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes; Rob adds that French words in de- or des- often carry Latin [[see:dis-]] through a French filter.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists as basic and easy to guess.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes; as im-, meaning not, it begins [[gave:impervious]].
A high-yield Latin prefix whose B changes to match the next sound by [[see:assimilation]], as in [[gave:suspect]], [[gave:succeed]] and [[gave:suffer]].
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists as basic and easy to guess.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists as basic and easy to guess.
When a prefix changes to match the word it joins, as [[see:sub-]] does in [[see:suspect]] and [[see:suffer]], or [[see:ob-]] in [[see:occult]].
A rarer change where a sound is altered to avoid repeating it, as when Latin [[see:medidies]] became [[see:meridies]], giving [[see:meridian]].
From [[from:sub-]] and [[from:specere]], to be under observation, an example of [[see:assimilation]].
From [[from:sub-]] and [[from:cedere]], to come after, another example of [[see:assimilation]].
Rob's extra example of [[see:sub-]] changing by [[see:assimilation]].
From [[from:sub-]] and [[from:ferre]], to carry: to be under a burden.
Latin prefix meaning not or away, as in [[gave:distribute]]; French words beginning [[see:de-]] or des- carry it through a French filter.
From [[from:dis-]]: essentially to tribute away or broadly.
A hard-working Latin prefix, here toward or in front of, seen in [[gave:obvious]], [[gave:oblivion]], [[gave:obnoxious]], [[gave:obscure]] and, assimilated, [[gave:occult]].
From [[from:oblivio]], forgetfulness: sending something into oblivion wipes it into empty nothingness.
To erase or blot out writing, from [[from:ob-]] and [[from:litera]]; a similar idea to [[see:oblivion]].
Toward [[from:noxa]], hurt or injury; its Latin predecessor meant injurious, so today's sense of annoying is much softer.
Discussed in the episode about magic; its initial O is [[from:ob-]] changed by [[see:assimilation]].
From [[from:ob-]], in front of, and [[from:fuscare]], to make something dark.
From [[from:ob-]] and [[from:scurus]], covered, the same element found in [[same-root:chiaroscuro]].
Meaning bright dark, from the art episode; it shares its second element with [[same-root:obscure]].
A little-known word meaning to walk around, built with [[from:ob-]].
Sleepwalking; Rob reached for it after hearing [[see:obambulation]] but got muddled.
A Latin suffix, also -ible, found in Romance words like [[see:visible]] but freely added to Germanic stems in [[see:watchable]], [[see:winnable]] and [[see:knowable]].
A Romance word with [[see:-able]], unlike hybrids such as [[see:watchable]].
A Romance word with [[see:-able]], unlike hybrids such as [[see:watchable]].
A [[see:hybrid word]] putting Latin [[see:-able]] on a Germanic stem.
A [[see:hybrid word]] putting Latin [[see:-able]] on a Germanic stem.
A [[see:hybrid word]] putting Latin [[see:-able]] on a Germanic stem.
A word mixing elements from different languages, like [[see:watchable]] or [[see:interplanetary]]; avoiding them produced Latin-only coinages like [[see:intermundane]].
Another Latin suffix English adds to Germanic nouns, creating a [[see:hybrid word]].
A [[see:hybrid word]] of Latin [[from:inter-]] and Greek [[from:planet]]; [[see:intermundane]] was coined as a non-hybrid alternative.
The Latin half of the hybrid [[see:interplanetary]].
The Greek half of the hybrid [[see:interplanetary]].
An 18th-century non-hybrid alternative to [[see:interplanetary]], built with [[from:mundane]], worldly.
Meaning worldly, the element used in [[see:intermundane]].
Jess's example of suffixes that fit their stems: darkity would sound stupid, unlike a [[see:hybrid word]] such as [[see:watchable]].
Jess's example of suffixes that fit their stems: happity would sound stupid.
Discussed in a recent episode: octopodes follows Greek, octopi isn't the real Latin plural, so the hosts recommend octopuses.
One of the -us nouns that really does become -i, oculi, in the plural.
One of the -us nouns that really does become -i, alumni, in the plural.
One of the -us nouns that really does become -i, stimuli, in the plural.
Its Latin plural is also prospectus, not prospecti; English says prospectuses.
Its Latin plural is also status, not stati; English says statuses.
Its Latin plural is also apparatus, not apparati; some circles use that plural in English, as apparatuses sounds a bit odd.
The Latin noun categories Jess says explain why plurals like [[see:prospectus]] and [[see:status]] break the -us to -i rule.
Latin for body, whose plural is corpora rather than corpi.
Latin for hand, whose plural is also manus, not mani.
Plural of alga, with no English plural algas; algae is often used as a singular too.
A Latin plural, from [[from:agere]], meaning things to be done, but used as a singular instead of agendum; originally theological, alongside [[see:credenda]].
Things to be believed, paired with [[see:agenda]] in its original theological use.
Discussed in a previous episode as sharing a Latin root with [[same-root:actor]], [[same-root:agent]] and [[same-root:agenda]].
Shares a Latin root with [[same-root:agent]]: both are doers, one on the stage, the other on someone's behalf.
Shares a Latin root with [[same-root:actor]]: a doer acting on behalf of someone else.
Has a Latin plural that English never adopted; we only say bonuses.
Has a Latin plural that English never adopted; we only say viruses.
Another -us word whose Latin plural English never bothered to adopt.
In Latin a doorkeeper or porter, related to [[same-root:Janus]]; it later meant a school usher and, by the 1700s, a caretaker.
The two-faced god of doorways, related to [[same-root:janitor]] and the source of [[gave:January]].
Named after [[from:Janus]], the god connected to [[see:janitor]].
Originally a sandy place, of uncertain and possibly Etruscan origin, because Roman amphitheatres were strewn with sand to soak up blood.
From medieval Latin [[from:dies mali]]; first a noun in the phrase in the dismal, then an adjective in dismal day, a tautology meaning bad day day.
Two unlucky days a month in medieval calendars, also called [[equivalent:Egyptian days]], [[equivalent:dies aegri]] and [[equivalent:dies maledicti]]; later any gloomy day, giving [[gave:dismal]].
Another name for [[equivalent:dies mali]], supposedly because ancient Egyptian scholars calculated them or because of the story of the plagues.
Another name for the unlucky days of [[equivalent:dies mali]].
Another name for the unlucky days of [[equivalent:dies mali]].
4th-century Roman scribe whose work holds the earliest reference to [[see:dies mali]]; Jess loves that this makes it the [[see:fasti]] of Furius.
Roman calendar lists of official and religious events, where [[see:dies mali]] were recorded; Jess relishes the fasti of [[see:Furius Dionysius Filocalus]].
Days on which official business could be done, listed in the [[see:fasti]].
An extremely productive Latin root in English, behind the doublets [[gave:diary]] and [[gave:journal]] and the related [[gave:meridian]].
Originally meaning lasting one day, from [[from:dies]]; a doublet of [[same-root:journal]], also mentioned in a previous episode.
The word [[from:diurnal]] squeezed through French; a doublet of [[same-root:diary]], from [[from:dies]].
Originally noon or midday, from Latin [[from:meridies]], which became that from [[from:medidies]] by [[see:dissimilation]]; related to [[same-root:dies]].
A term poets sometimes use for midnight, from [[from:meridian]].
Covered in an earlier episode about legal terms.
